archetype.name: Pocket Passer (timing-and-accuracy)
archetype.definition: Burrow wins from the pocket with anticipation and ball placement rather than arm theatrics or legs, and he is at his best attacking the 10-to-19-yard window on time.

report.headline: Winning in the 10-to-19 range; the short game is what's holding him back.
report.take:
Burrow has always been an accuracy-first pocket passer. He led the position in CPOE in 2021, ranked 5th in 2024 and posted the lowest bad-throw rate of any qualifier in 2025. He gets the ball out in roughly 2.5 to 2.8 seconds and rarely needs his legs. The 2026 version fits that template: 71.3% completions (5th), a 7.6% bad-throw rate (6th of 32) and 2.57 seconds to throw. What has changed over time is his willingness to fit balls into tight windows. His aggressiveness has fallen from 21.5% as a rookie to 12.74% now, and his throws arrive on average 1.62 yards short of the sticks.

The season is really two different quarterbacks. On 54 intermediate and deep attempts he has been outstanding. The 42 throws of 10 to 19 yards carry +0.98 EPA, a 76.2% success rate and a CPOE of 19.3. The 12 deep shots are worth +1.689 EPA each and have produced 3 of his 7 touchdowns, though that is a small sample. On the 103 throws behind the line or under 10 yards, the offense is losing points. Screens and swings sit at -0.323 EPA, and short throws sit at -0.239 with all 3 interceptions. Chase Brown's 24 targets have returned -0.267 EPA per target. That split explains how he can rank 5th in yards but 19th in EPA per dropback. The volume is structural: Cincinnati passes more than situation predicts by the widest margin in the league, and its run game ranks 18th in EPA.

The totals also blur a sharp upward path. The first two weeks combined for -3.1 passing EPA. The Houston game was the low point: 5 sacks, 30.6% pressured and a 19.4% bad-throw rate. The last two weeks combined for +22.1. Protection is a team problem, with the offense's QB hit rate ranking 28th. Burrow is handling it better than ever, though: his 25.9% pressure-to-sack rate is lower than in any of his six previous seasons. The weak spots are late-game splits. He has -0.274 EPA on 31 plays leading by 9 or more and -0.179 on 27 fourth-quarter plays in close games, and both losses came by a field goal or less than a touchdown. Those samples are thin, but they are where the 2-2 record came from. His 4.5% TD rate (22nd) sits well below his career norms and should climb.

The forward question is personnel. His downfield efficiency runs through Tee Higgins (39 targets, +0.632 EPA per target) and Ja'Marr Chase (+0.562). Chase left Week 4 with a concussion and Higgins is day-to-day with a groin issue. Burrow still threw for 428 yards after Chase left that game, and Mike Gesicki has been the most efficient target of all on a small sample (+1.015 per target on 15). The arc is rising, but how high depends on who is on the field.

strengths.title: Intermediate and deep precision
strengths.body: His throws of 10 or more air yards are completing far above expectation and turning into points at an extreme rate. This is his career calling card, a timing passer who throws receivers open over the middle and outside the numbers. The intermediate edge should hold. The deep EPA on 12 attempts will cool, but it does not need to stay this high to carry the offense.

strengths.title: Accuracy without the sack tax
strengths.body: He completes passes at a top-five rate with few bad throws. This year he is also taking fewer sacks once pressured than at any point in his career, which matters behind a line that lets him get hit often. Both the accuracy and the low bad-throw rate have held across seasons, so they are sustainable traits rather than a hot streak.

strengths.title: League's most pass-tilted offense
strengths.body: Cincinnati passes more than game situations call for by the widest margin in the league. That keeps his attempts and yardage high regardless of efficiency swings. With the run game ranked 18th in EPA, there is no reason to expect that tilt to change.

concerns.title: Top two receivers both banged up
concerns.body: Higgins and Chase account for 67 targets at more than +0.5 EPA each, and they carry the downfield game that drives his efficiency. Chase is in the concussion process after leaving Week 4, and Higgins is day-to-day with a groin issue. Losing either one shifts volume to targets who have been far less productive, outside of Gesicki's small sample. This is a real, near-term risk to his ceiling, not a flaw in his game.

concerns.title: Short game is costing points
concerns.body: Throws behind the line and under 10 yards are negative-EPA plays, and all 3 interceptions came there. Running-back targets have been the worst of it. Some of this is scheme and his lower aggressiveness, since he is throwing short of the sticks on average. The interceptions on short throws look more like variance than a trend. Still, the low-value checkdowns are a design issue that will persist unless the offense changes how it uses the short area.

concerns.title: Protection lets him get hit
concerns.body: The offense ranks near the bottom in QB hit rate, and he is hit or sacked on nearly a fifth of dropbacks. The Houston game showed the downside: 5 sacks and a spike in bad throws. His quick release and low sack conversion soften the problem, but this is a line issue that will resurface against good fronts.

trend.note: Passing EPA has gone from -2.6 and -0.5 in the first two games to +14.7 at Pittsburgh and +7.4 against Jacksonville. He has opened up his air yards (8.8 intended in Week 4) as the season has gone on.

nextGame.headline: Leaky Miami pass defense sets up well, if his receivers play
nextGame.body:
Miami's defense ranks 29th in pass EPA allowed and 28th in sack rate. It is also 29th against short passes, which is exactly the area where Cincinnati's passing game has been bleeding value. A defense that gives up efficient short completions and rarely gets home is the best possible setting for his quick-game reads to start paying off. Miami is sturdier against the run (9th in EPA), which reinforces Cincinnati's pass-first lean. Its offense ranks 30th in EPA and 31st in success rate, so Burrow should get plenty of possessions. The risk is the game script: as a 7-point favorite he may spend time protecting a lead, and that has been his weakest split.

Burrow himself is listed active as QB1, and the only practice report in the dossier dates to Week 2, when he was a full participant, so there is no current concern about him. The availability that matters is his receivers. Chase is in concussion protocol and Higgins is day-to-day, and their status decides whether he can keep attacking the intermediate window. Colbie Young's absence barely matters at 11% of snaps. On Miami's side, starting safety Dante Trader Jr. (73% of snaps) is questionable, and missing him would thin the coverage behind the corners. Edge rusher Robert Beal Jr. is out, which takes something off an already weak rush. Corners Reese Taylor and Storm Duck are out, but neither has played this season, so nothing changes there.

keyMatchups.title: Quick game vs. soft underneath coverage
keyMatchups.body: Cincinnati's short throws have been a liability, while Miami allows some of the most efficient short passing in the league. If the underneath game finally produces positive plays here, his efficiency jumps. If it doesn't, the short-game problem is more about design than opponents.

keyMatchups.title: Weak Miami rush meets leaky line
keyMatchups.body: Cincinnati's line allows a high hit rate, but Miami rarely sacks the quarterback and is without a rotational edge rusher. This should be one of his cleaner pockets of the season.

keyMatchups.title: Playing with a lead
keyMatchups.body: A 7-point spread against the league's 30th-ranked offense points to Cincinnati leading for long stretches. That is where Burrow's EPA has turned negative, on a small sample of 31 plays. Expect fewer late attempts if the game breaks open.

nextGame.watch: Whether Chase clears concussion protocol and Higgins plays: with both, his intermediate game should carve up Miami; without them, the offense leans on the short game that has been losing points.

restOfSeason.body:
The core of this season should hold: top-tier accuracy, a quick release and the league's most pass-heavy offense. His 4.5% TD rate is the clearest candidate to rise toward his career norms, because he has been scoring from deep rather than piling up short red-zone touchdowns. The short-throw interceptions should also thin out.

The deep EPA will cool from its current level on just 12 attempts, and the 428-yard, 54-attempt game inflates his yardage average. Without it he averaged about 248 yards. Expect efficiency to keep improving as the first-two-weeks drag washes out, with yardage settling a bit below the current 293 per game. All of that depends on Chase and Higgins staying healthy. His own durability is also a factor: three of his six seasons ended before 11 games.
swingFactors: Whether the short and RB passing game stops losing EPA

bets.reason: Miami ranks 28th in sack rate and 23rd in hit rate and is without edge rusher Beal. Burrow's pressure-to-sack rate is the lowest of his career, and outside the 5-sack Houston game he has taken 1 or 2 sacks per game.

Miami's offense ranks 30th in EPA and 31st in success rate, while Cincinnati's defense is 2nd in sack rate and Miami's pass defense is 29th. The edge is tempered by Chase's and Higgins' uncertain status and by Cincinnati's 0-2 ATS record as a favorite.
Miami allows 2 passing TDs a game to quarterbacks and ranks 29th in pass EPA. His low TD rate looks due to rise, given how efficient he has been in the intermediate and deep areas.

bets.market: Burrow passing yards over his 293-a-game average
bets.reason: His average is inflated by a 54-attempt, 428-yard game in a loss. As a 7-point favorite he projects to throw less late in the game, and Miami allows a middling 244.8 yards per game to quarterbacks.

confidence.note: Four-game sample with a sharp early-to-late split, and both top receivers' availability is unresolved.
